title: Just published in Nature Methods – Large-scale single-molecule analysis of tau proteoforms
summary: Watch our new video series for insights from the large-scale single-molecule analysis of proteoforms.
body_markdown:
We are incredibly proud to announce that our paper covering the large-scale single-molecule analysis of tau proteoforms by Iterative Mapping has been published in Nature Methods!


[https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-026-03188-6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-026-03188-6)


This work demonstrates the technical power of single-molecule proteomic analysis on the Nautilus Voyager™ Platform. It further shows that single-molecule proteomic analysis reveals entirely new facets of biology. Specifically:


- **Iterative Mapping enables accessible and scalable proteoform analysis that is not possible on any other platform** . Proteoforms are the distinct molecular forms of proteins that exist in cells. Many can be derived from a single protein and may have vastly different functions depending on their combinations of isoforms, sequence variations, and post-translational modifications.
- **Iterative Mapping precisely, sensitively, and accurately quantifies tau proteoforms over a wide dynamic range with high reproducibility (≤5.5% median CV).** These exceptional quantitative characteristics make the data generated on the platform particularly trustworthy.
- **Model systems commonly used in neurodegenerative disease research have distinct tau proteoform profiles.** These profiles may help reveal which aspects of neurodegeneration each system is suited to model.
- **In a small cohort, tau proteoform analysis differentiates samples originating from cognitively normal individuals and individuals with Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias.** In the future, tau proteoform analyses like these may make it possible to diagnose different stages of neurodegenerative diseases. Some of these tau proteoforms may also make valuable drug targets.
- **Preliminary evidence suggests ordered pathways underlie the creation of tau proteoforms (they are not created randomly)** . This implies researchers may be able to prevent the generation of pathological tau proteoforms by disrupting these pathways!


To help you get the most from the publication, we’re launching a new video series. In it, Nautilus Co-Founder Parag Mallick and the paper’s first authors will walk you through the paper’s key findings and their significance.
